paper: AudioJudge: Understanding What Works in Large Audio Model Based Speech Evaluation
what_it_does: Systematic study of large audio models (LAMs) as judges of speech: pronunciation match, speaking rate, speaker ID, speech quality, and pairwise human-preference simulation over TTS system outputs; tests prompting strategies (audio concatenation, ICL, multi-aspect ensembles).
results: Multi-aspect ensemble judge reaches 0.91 Spearman with human system rankings; judges show significant verbosity and positional bias; robust to acoustic noise.
drawbacks: Evaluees are TTS/LAM systems, not human speakers; only degradations tested are noise/verbosity/position, never evaluee identity.
gap_vs_ours: Never varies the evaluee's voice identity (accent/gender/delivery) while holding content fixed; this is the judge-bias framework we extend.

paper: Auditing Protocol-Level Shortcuts in Large Audio Language Model Judges for Speech Evaluation
what_it_does: Audits whether LALM judges genuinely analyze audio or exploit protocol shortcuts (feature-blueprint text, reference conditioning, A/B slot position) across six judges and four attributes.
results: Incorrect feature labels sharply degrade blueprint judging; some models show slot-preference bias regardless of order.
drawbacks: Treatment is the evaluation protocol's structure/text, not the speaker.
gap_vs_ours: No evaluee-voice manipulation at all; purely a protocol-shortcut audit.

paper: ParaPairAudioBench: Paralinguistic Pairwise Audio Benchmark for LALM-as-a-Judge
what_it_does: 5,175 audio pairs testing LALM judges on five paralinguistic dimensions (Style, Rate, Emphasis, Age, Gender), with same-transcript vs cross-transcript conditions to separate lexical from acoustic reliance.
results: LALM judges lag human judgment by ~32 points on average, with severe calibration failures especially on ties.
drawbacks: Tests whether judges can correctly PERCEIVE/RANK paralinguistic differences as the judging target, not whether those attributes leak into an unrelated content score.
gap_vs_ours: Measures judge competence at detecting gender/age, not whether accent/gender contaminate a content-quality grade of a fixed answer.

paper: SpeechLLM-as-Judges: Towards General and Interpretable Speech Quality Evaluation
what_it_does: Builds SpeechEval (32,207 clips, 128,754 annotations) and trains SQ-LLM, a chain-of-thought speech-quality judge across 4 tasks and multiple languages.
results: SQ-LLM gives strong cross-task, cross-lingual quality judgments with structured explanations.
drawbacks: Optimizes judge accuracy/interpretability; no fairness axis at all.
gap_vs_ours: No counterfactual test of speaker identity effects on scores.

paper: JASTIN: Aligning LLMs for Zero-Shot Audio and Speech Evaluation via Natural Language Instructions
what_it_does: Frozen audio encoder + fine-tuned LLM via trainable adapter for instruction-driven zero-shot audio/speech/music quality assessment.
results: State-of-the-art Pearson/Spearman correlation with human subjective ratings without task-specific retraining.
drawbacks: Pure judge-construction work.
gap_vs_ours: No fairness or voice-identity manipulation of the evaluee at all.

paper: VIBE: Voice-Induced Open-ended Bias Evaluation for Large Audio-Language Models via Real-World Speech
what_it_does: Evaluates generative bias in 12 audio-LLMs on open-ended tasks (e.g. personalized recommendations) using human-recorded speech including L2-ARCTIC for accent, rejecting synthetic-speech+MCQ benchmarks as fragmented.
results: Gender and accent cues in the user's voice cause statistically significant distributional shifts in what the model generates; effect is task-dependent.
drawbacks: Outcome is what the ASSISTANT generates/recommends for the speaker, not a grade assigned to the speaker's own answer; no TTS arm despite using real L2-ARCTIC speech.
gap_vs_ours: Uses our exact real-speech corpus but for the assistant-generation-bias question, not judge-scoring of evaluee content; validates L2-ARCTIC as a credible instrument for us.

paper: Do Audio Language Models Use Paralinguistic Evidence? Counterfactual Audits for Response Evaluation
what_it_does: Counterfactual audits on audio-LLM JUDGES that hold the transcript fixed while varying affect, prosody, or the timing of an affective shift, testing whether judges rely on audio evidence at all (Gemini, GPT, open models).
results: Contrastive success often overstates native judge reliability; behavioral audits should precede deployment.
drawbacks: Varied factor is affect/prosody for evidence-use correctness, not accent/gender/code-switching as a demographic bias treatment on content scores.
gap_vs_ours: Closest methodological cousin (transcript-fixed, multi-judge-family counterfactual protocol on judges) but tests evidence-use, not identity-driven score bias.

paper: Bias in the Ear of the Listener: Assessing Sensitivity in Audio Language Models Across Linguistic, Demographic, and Positional Variations (BiasInEar)
what_it_does: Multilingual (EN/ZH/KO) speech-augmented Global MMLU Lite benchmark (~11,200 questions); evaluates 9 audio LLMs on QA accuracy/entropy/APES/Fleiss-kappa under linguistic, demographic (voice), and positional variation of the QUESTION audio.
results: Models are relatively robust to demographic (accent/gender) factors but highly sensitive to language and option order.
drawbacks: Model is the TEST-TAKER, not a judge; voice varies the question, not an evaluee's answer; TTS-only (Gemini 2.5 Flash TTS), no real speech.
gap_vs_ours: No judging role, no evaluee, no score assigned to any speaker's content.

paper: The Voice Behind the Words: Quantifying Intersectional Bias in SpeechLLMs
what_it_does: 2,880 controlled interactions across 6 English accents x 2 gender presentations (voice-cloned questions to 3 SpeechLLMs); rates the SPEECHLLM's own text response via pointwise LLM-judge, pairwise, and BWS, validated against humans.
results: Eastern-European-accented speech gets lower assistant helpfulness scores, worst for female-presenting voices; LLM judges underdetect disparities humans see.
drawbacks: THE JUDGE IS TEXT-ONLY AND EXPLICITLY VOICE-BLIND ('the judge receives only the user question and the SpeechLLM response, with no knowledge of the speech accent, gender, or hesitation metadata' -- Sec 3.2). Voice varies the QUESTION-ASKER; judge never hears audio; outcome is the assistant's own generated reply, not a grade on a fixed evaluee answer.
gap_vs_ours: CLOSEST paper by topic but structurally orthogonal to our claim: it shows the assistant behaves differently toward differently-voiced users, filtered through a blinded text judge -- it cannot and does not show that an audio-input judge's SCORE of an evaluee's ANSWER shifts with that evaluee's voice. This is the paper our novelty-delineation section must address most carefully.

paper: From Seeing it to Experiencing it: Interactive Evaluation of Intersectional Voice Bias in Human-AI Speech Interaction
what_it_does: Companion to 2603.16941: controlled cohort (6 accents x 2 genders) plus interactive user study (N=24) using voice conversion so users experience identical content through different vocal identities; explicitly judge-free.
results: Voice conversion raises trust/acceptability; reveals accent x gender disparities in assistant alignment and verbosity.
drawbacks: Explicitly judge-free by design; measures human user experience and assistant QoS, not any model's evaluative score.
gap_vs_ours: No judge in the loop at all; not our niche.

paper: Evaluating Bias in Spoken Dialogue LLMs for Real-World Decisions and Recommendations (FairDialogue)
what_it_does: Measures how paralinguistic cues (age, gender, accent) in synthesized speech shift decision/recommendation outputs of spoken dialogue models (Qwen2.5-Omni, GLM-4-Voice, GPT-4o Audio, Gemini 2.5 Flash), including multi-turn dialogue.
results: Proprietary models show lower bias; open-source models more sensitive to age/gender; recommendation tasks amplify disparities; bias persists across turns.
drawbacks: Model is an ADVISOR producing its own recommendation for the speaker, not a grader of the speaker's answer content; TTS-only, no real-speech anchor.
gap_vs_ours: Advisor role, not judge role; outcome is generated advice, not a rubric score of fixed content.

paper: Audio-Aware Large Language Models as Judges for Speaking Styles
what_it_does: Uses GPT-4o-audio and Gemini-2.5-pro as judges of SYNTHETIC assistant speech style (emotion, volume, pace, emphasis, pitch, non-verbals) vs human evaluators.
results: Gemini-human agreement comparable to human-human agreement on style judging.
drawbacks: Judges style-quality of the assistant's OWN generated speech; no evaluee identity manipulation; no content-quality scoring under identity variation.
gap_vs_ours: Different object of judgment entirely (assistant's synthetic voice-style output, not a human evaluee's answer content).

paper: Audio Large Language Models Can Be Descriptive Speech Quality Evaluators
what_it_does: Natural-language speech-quality corpus and ALLD (alignment with LLM distillation) method so audio LLMs extract MOS-relevant information from raw speech.
results: 0.17 MSE on MOS prediction, 98.6% A/B test accuracy, beating prior models.
drawbacks: Trains a better acoustic-quality judge; never tests speaker-demographic effects on scores of identical content.
gap_vs_ours: No accent/gender/identity treatment; pure judge-capability engineering.

paper: Bias Analysis of L2 Speaking Assessment Systems Using Concept Activation Vectors
what_it_does: Uses Concept Activation Vectors and sparse autoencoders to probe whether a BERT text grader and Whisper-based multimodal grader of L2 speaking internally ENCODE irrelevant speaker attributes (L1, age).
results: Concept recoverability strongly depends on representation/architecture probed; encoding a concept is distinct from it influencing the predicted score.
drawbacks: Interpretability probing of internal representations on naturally-varying speakers, not a causal audit; never swaps voice on identical content.
gap_vs_ours: Model is a grader, but the audit is correlational/representational, not a controlled same-content voice-swap experiment.

paper: Speak Your Mind: The Speech Continuation Task as a Probe of Voice-Based Model Bias
what_it_does: First systematic bias assessment of speech CONTINUATION across gender and phonation styles, testing SpiritLM, VAE-GSLM, SpeechGPT.
results: Significant model x gender interactions; continuations shift toward modal/standard phonation more for female speakers.
drawbacks: Generative continuation behavior, not evaluation; no judge, no scores.
gap_vs_ours: Not a judging task at all.

paper: Do Bias Benchmarks Generalise? Evidence from Voice-based Evaluation of Gender Bias in SpeechLLMs
what_it_does: LoRA-fine-tunes 3 SpeechLLMs to hold specific MCQA gender-bias preferences, then tests whether that behavior transfers to other MCQA benchmarks and long-form generation.
results: MCQA bias-benchmark performance fails to predict bias in other benchmarks or long-form tasks.
drawbacks: Meta-methodological critique of assistant-role bias benchmarks; no grading task.
gap_vs_ours: Does not test the model as grader; voice identity is not a treatment on assigned scores.

paper: Acoustic-based Gender Differentiation in Speech-aware Language Models
what_it_does: 9,208 speech samples probing whether identical questions get different answers by speaker gender in the LLaMA-Omni series; traces mechanism to the audio encoder.
results: Paradox: male-oriented answers on gender-stereotypical questions but gender-blind answers where differentiation is appropriate; traced to the Whisper encoder producing male-oriented acoustic tokens.
drawbacks: Assistant-role response differentiation to the speaker's own query; no grading task, no score on content-identical answers.
gap_vs_ours: Useful mechanism reference (encoder leaks speaker identity) but no judge, no evaluee-answer scoring.

paper: Interpretable, Fairly Evaluated Automated L2 Speaking Assessment that Beats the Single-Human Ceiling
what_it_does: Hybrid speech-timing-features + text-LLM fluency grader for spontaneous L2 dialogue (130 ICNALE speeches) validated against 80 trained human raters, with a per-L1 fairness audit.
results: Spearman rho=0.818, exceeding 81% of individual human raters; explicit pause encoding gives no scoring advantage over aggregate pause statistics.
drawbacks: Fairness audit is OBSERVATIONAL across naturally different speakers producing different content -- not a causal same-content voice swap; model is a bespoke hybrid scorer, not a general audio-LLM judge.
gap_vs_ours: Real L2 speech + grader + fairness axis, but correlational, not causal; no code-switching, no delivery treatment, no audio-LLM battery.

paper: Assessment of L2 Oral Proficiency using Speech Large Language Models
what_it_does: Fine-tunes multimodal speech LLMs to grade L2 English speaking proficiency, comparing regression vs classification targets and cross-task transfer.
results: Speech LLMs beat prior competitive baselines on two L2 datasets and generalize across test parts/tasks.
drawbacks: Optimizes grading accuracy; never manipulates evaluee voice identity on content-identical answers.
gap_vs_ours: No causal identity manipulation at all; pure capability paper.

paper: Evaluating Speech-to-Text x LLM x Text-to-Speech Combinations for AI Interview Systems
what_it_does: Large empirical comparison of cascaded STT/LLM/TTS stacks over 300,000+ real AI-conducted job interviews using an LLM-as-judge evaluation framework.
results: Google STT + GPT-4.1 + Cartesia TTS performs best; objective quality metrics correlate only weakly with user satisfaction.
drawbacks: Documents our exact deployment surface (AI interview pipelines with LLM judging) but optimizes component choice only.
gap_vs_ours: No fairness or evaluee-identity manipulation of any kind; motivates our 'why it matters' section, not a competing result.

paper: Integrating Psychometrics and Computing Perspectives on Bias and Fairness in Affective Computing: A Case Study of Automated Video Interviews
what_it_does: Merges psychometric and ML fairness frameworks to catalogue bias sources in inferring personality/hireability from multimodal automated video interview data.
results: Provides fairness/bias measurement methods and metrics for automated interview assessment pipelines.
drawbacks: Framework + observational fairness metrics on pre-LLM multimodal features; no audio-LLM judge.
gap_vs_ours: Pre-audio-LLM era framework paper; no controlled content-identical voice manipulation.

paper: Do LLM Decoders Listen Fairly? Benchmarking How Language Model Priors Shape Bias in Speech Recognition
what_it_does: Benchmarks 9 models across 3 architectures on ~43k utterances over 5 demographic dimensions (ethnicity, accent, gender, age, L1) to test whether LLM decoders amplify ASR bias, including acoustic-stress conditions.
results: LLM decoders don't amplify racial bias; Whisper hallucinates selectively on Indian-accented speech, worsened by silence injection; audio encoder design (not LLM scale) is the fairness lever.
drawbacks: Establishes the upstream ASR/transcription channel of accent bias but stops at recognition (WER), never at downstream evaluative scoring.
gap_vs_ours: Motivates our acoustic-vs-ASR-channel decomposition arm; is the ASR-side analog we cite, not a competing result.

paper: Racial disparities in automated speech recognition
what_it_does: Audits 5 commercial ASR systems (Amazon, Apple, Google, IBM, Microsoft) on 19.8h of interviews with 42 white and 73 Black speakers, age/gender matched, including some identical phrases.
results: Average WER 0.35 for Black vs 0.19 for white speakers; gap persists on identical phrases, traced to acoustic models.
drawbacks: Canonical upstream ASR-disparity result even using matched-content phrases, but measures transcription error, not judge-assigned scores.
gap_vs_ours: Cited as the classic ASR-channel precedent our decomposition arm builds on.

paper: VoiceAgentBench: Are Voice Assistants ready for agentic tasks?
what_it_does: Benchmarks SpeechLMs on 6,000+ synthetic agentic spoken queries in English + 6 Indic languages (tool calls, multi-tool orchestration, dialogue, safety), using voice-conversion for speaker diversity.
results: ASR-LLM pipelines hit ~60.6% on English tool invocation; end-to-end models degrade sharply on Indic languages; gaps in tool coordination and adversarial robustness.
drawbacks: Speaker diversity is a robustness augmentation, not a causally analyzed bias factor; covers agentic task-completion competence, not evaluative scoring.
gap_vs_ours: Owns the agentic/Indic-benchmark space; explicitly out of scope for us -- cited to delineate our optional code-switching arm from its territory.

paper: Reverse Linguistic Stereotyping: Measuring the Effect of Listener Expectations on Speech Evaluation
what_it_does: Classic guise experiment: listeners rate the SAME recorded speech paired with different apparent speaker identities (e.g., White vs Asian face) to isolate expectation-driven bias.
results: Identical native-English audio was rated more accented and less comprehensible under the Asian-guise condition; listener expectations alone shift speech evaluations.
drawbacks: Human listeners, not LLM judges; predates audio-LLMs entirely.
gap_vs_ours: The exact human-rater precedent for our design -- content-identical audio + manipulated identity -- that we port from human listeners to audio-LLM judges; strong motivating citation.

paper: MedVoiceBias: A Controlled Study of Audio LLM Behavior in Clinical Decision-Making
what_it_does: Synthesizes 170 clinical cases into speech from 36 TTS voice profiles varying age, gender, emotion; compares audio-LLM clinical recommendations vs identical text inputs.
results: Severe modality bias (surgical recommendations shift up to 35% audio vs text); age disparities up to 12% persist under chain-of-thought; explicit reasoning removes gender bias.
drawbacks: TTS-only stimuli, no real-speech anchor; outcome is clinical decisions, not judge scores of an evaluee's answer quality; no accent axis.
gap_vs_ours: Adjacent domain (clinical decisions, not grading); supports our TTS-as-instrument approach but doesn't compete with our judge-role claim.

paper: Position: Towards Responsible Evaluation for Text-to-Speech
what_it_does: Position paper arguing current TTS evaluation is inadequate; proposes a three-level 'Responsible Evaluation' framework (faithful capability measurement, standardized benchmarks, societal-impact/bias assessment).
results: Argues existing TTS scoring methodologies fail to reflect true capabilities and that bias/misuse dimensions are unmeasured.
drawbacks: Critique of how TTS itself is evaluated, not a use of TTS as a controlled instrument to audit downstream audio-LLM judges.
gap_vs_ours: Supports our instrument-validity caution (manipulation-check requirement) but is not a competing empirical result.

paper: Pairwise Evaluation of Accent Similarity in Speech Synthesis
what_it_does: Builds subjective (refined XAB with transcripts) and objective (vowel-formant distance, phonetic posteriorgrams) methods for evaluating accent similarity of accented TTS output.
results: Pronunciation-based + acoustic metrics are jointly usable for accent-similarity evaluation; WER has significant limitations for underrepresented accents.
drawbacks: Evaluates TTS output quality itself, not effects on any downstream judge.
gap_vs_ours: Provides exactly the accent-fidelity manipulation-check methodology our TTS treatment arm needs; a methods citation, not a competing result.

paper: CodecMOS-Accent: A MOS Benchmark of Resynthesized and TTS Speech from Neural Codecs Across English Accents
what_it_does: MOS benchmark of 4,000 codec-resynthesis and TTS samples from 24 systems, 32 speakers, 10 accents; 19,600 human annotations on naturalness, speaker similarity, accent similarity.
results: Tight coupling between speaker similarity and accent similarity; documents listener perceptual bias effects on accent ratings.
drawbacks: Quantifies TTS/codec accent fidelity (instrument validation) but has no audio-LLM judge and no causal scoring outcome.
gap_vs_ours: Instrument-validity citation for our manipulation check, not a competing empirical claim.

paper: Scalable Controllable Accented TTS
what_it_does: Scales accented TTS via speech-geolocation-based accent label discovery plus kNN voice-conversion timbre augmentation, fine-tuning XTTS-v2 on CommonVoice.
results: Geolocation-discovered accent labels beat self-reported labels and existing accented-TTS benchmarks.
drawbacks: Establishes that accent-controllable TTS is nontrivial and label-dependent; does no bias auditing of any downstream model.
gap_vs_ours: A validity caveat for our Gemini/ElevenLabs accent prompting -- motivates our mandatory manipulation-check pilot.

paper: VocalBench-DF: A Benchmark for Evaluating Speech LLM Robustness to Disfluency
what_it_does: Framework for evaluating speech-LLM robustness to disfluency across a multi-dimensional taxonomy (motivated by Parkinson's-type impairments); evaluates 22 mainstream Speech-LLMs.
results: Substantial performance degradation under disfluency; phoneme-level processing and long-context modeling are the primary bottlenecks.
drawbacks: Treats disfluency as a robustness stressor on TASK PERFORMANCE, not as a delivery treatment on judge SCORES of content-identical answers.
gap_vs_ours: Delineates our delivery arm: comprehension robustness (their claim) vs. grading-score leakage under an ignore-delivery instruction (our claim).

paper: Investigating Human-Model Discrepancies in Speech Quality Assessment via Acoustic and Prosodic Perturbations
what_it_does: Applies controlled perturbations (acoustic degradation, prosodic errors, pitch/rate manipulation) and compares MOS-prediction models against human listeners.
results: Models track acoustic degradation but are insensitive to prosodic errors humans penalize; strong mean-F0 biases absent in humans.
drawbacks: Targets speech-quality (MOS) models, not audio-LLM content judges; no accent/identity variables.
gap_vs_ours: Validates our controlled-perturbation methodology for the delivery arm; a methods citation.

paper: Should We Type or Talk to LLM Agents? A Comprehensive Study of Voice and Keyboard Input Perturbations (HIVE)
what_it_does: Introduces HIVE, voice-transcription and keyboard perturbation suites; evaluates instruction-tuned LLM robustness to each channel's noise signature.
results: Voice perturbations lower accuracy across all models; transcription structure (not filler words) carries most of the cost.
drawbacks: Perturbs text transcripts fed to text LLMs; never touches audio-LLM judges or speaker identity.
gap_vs_ours: Supports our WER-neutral-filler design choice; not a judge-bias result.

paper: L2-ARCTIC: A Non-native English Speech Corpus
what_it_does: Canonical corpus paper: non-native English read speech on CMU ARCTIC prompts from 10 (later 24) speakers across Hindi/Korean/Mandarin/Spanish/Arabic/Vietnamese L1s, with orthographic/phonetic alignments and 150 manually annotated utterances per speaker.
results: Built for voice conversion, accent conversion, and mispronunciation detection research; now the standard real-L2 accent testbed.
drawbacks: No bias auditing in the original paper.
gap_vs_ours: The corpus itself -- our causal real-speech anchor; license (CC BY-NC 4.0) and 1,132-sentence overlap with CMU ARCTIC independently verified for this project (2026-09-03).

paper: Prior over Evidence: Stereotype-Driven Diagnosis in LLM-Based L2 Pronunciation Feedback
what_it_does: Tests 1,800 L2-ARCTIC utterances across six L1 backgrounds on three audio-capable LLMs used to give pronunciation feedback grounded in externally computed evidence.
results: General-purpose LLMs are more reliable as verbalizers of externally computed pronunciation evidence than as standalone diagnostic engines; stereotype-driven diagnosis errors documented.
drawbacks: Shares our real-L2-ARCTIC instrument and accent(L1) axis and a judge/diagnostic role, but measures diagnostic grounding accuracy, not whether a held-constant CONTENT score shifts with voice; no gender, delivery, or code-switching axis; no TTS-vs-real-L2 crossing.
gap_vs_ours: Nearest neighbor by instrument (shares L2-ARCTIC + audio-LLM-as-evaluator), but the outcome variable is diagnostic accuracy/stereotyping in feedback generation, not a content-quality score of a fixed answer.

paper: MOS-Bias: From Hidden Gender Bias to Gender-Aware Speech Quality Assessment
what_it_does: Documents systematic gender bias in human Mean Opinion Score (MOS) annotation of speech quality and proposes gender-aware assessment methods.
results: Male listeners consistently assign higher MOS scores than female listeners across corpora.
drawbacks: Rater-gender bias in human MOS annotation, not evaluee-voice bias in an LLM judge's content grading.
gap_vs_ours: Different axis entirely (annotator demographics, not evaluee demographics); cited only to delineate our scope.
